## Motivation

**Lagrangian mechanics** is a reformulation of [[classical-mechanics]] that
describes a mechanical system through a single scalar function of positions and
velocities, instead of forces. It is equivalent to Newton's laws and to
[[hamiltonian-mechanics]], but takes the same form in any system of
coordinates.

Recall that a system of $N$ point masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}$ with Cartesian
positions $\vec{r}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^3$ and velocities
$\vec{v}_{i}=\dot{\vec{r}}_{i}$ obeys Newton's second law
$$
\vec F_i=m_i\ddot{\vec{r}}_i,
$$
which is a system of $3N$ second-order
[[ordinary-differential-equations]]. Lagrangian mechanics avoids forces and
considers energies. In the absence of an electromagnetic field the
non-relativistic **Lagrangian** is the difference of kinetic energy $K$ and
potential energy $U$,
$$
\mathcal{L}=K-U,\qquad K=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=1}^{N}m_{k}\lVert\vec v_{k}\rVert^2.
$$
The kinetic energy depends only on velocities, and for conservative forces
(e.g. gravity) the potential energy depends only on positions.

## Configuration Space and Action

Rather than Cartesian coordinates we use **generalised coordinates**
$\boldsymbol{q}$ and their rates of change $\dot{\boldsymbol{q}}$. For $N$
particles in $\mathbb{R}^3$ the **configuration space** is a smooth manifold
$Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{3N}$, each point $q\in Q$ specifying the admissible
positions of all particles at one instant. A **trajectory** is a smooth
function $q:[t_{0},t_{1}]\to Q$. The **tangent bundle** $TQ$ of $Q$ contains
the pairs $(q,\dot q)$ of positions and velocities.

:::{.definition data-title="Lagrangian"}

A **Lagrangian** is a smooth function $\mathcal{L}:TQ\times\mathbb{R}\to
\mathbb{R}$, $(q,\dot q,t)\mapsto\mathcal{L}(q,\dot q,t)$, with units of
energy.

:::

:::{.definition data-title="Action"}

The **action** of a trajectory $q$ is the integral of the Lagrangian along it,
$$
\mathscr{A}[q]=\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\mathcal{L}(q(t),\dot{q}(t),t)~dt.
$$
It is a functional: a map from functions to real numbers (see
[[calculus-of-variations]]).

:::

The laws of motion follow from **Hamilton's principle of stationary action**:
among all trajectories between two given configurations, the one actually
taken is a critical point (often, but not necessarily, a minimum) of the
action. By the [[calculus-of-variations]] this is equivalent to the
[[euler-lagrange-equation]].

:::{.theorem data-title="Euler-Lagrange Equations"}

A trajectory $q$ that is a critical point of $\mathscr{A}$ satisfies, for each
coordinate $q_i$,
$$
\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\dot q_i}
=\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial q_i}.
$$

:::

The quantity $p_i=\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\dot q_i$ is the **generalised
momentum** and $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial q_i$ the **generalised force**,
so the equations read "rate of change of momentum equals force", recovering
Newton's second law. In particular, if $\mathcal{L}$ does not depend on $q_i$
(a **cyclic** coordinate) then $p_i$ is conserved. The map from $(q,\dot q)$
to $(q,p)$ leads to [[hamiltonian-mechanics]].

## Example: The Pendulum

:::{.example data-title="Pendulum"}

Consider a frictionless pendulum: a mass $m$ on a rigid massless rod of length
$l$, with $\theta$ the angle from the downward vertical. The arc length is
$s=l\theta$, so the kinetic energy is
$$
K=\frac{1}{2}m\dot s^2=\frac{1}{2}ml^2\dot\theta^2.
$$
Measuring height from the pivot, the bob is at height $-l\cos\theta$, so
$U=-mgl\cos\theta$ and
$$
\mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{2}ml^2\dot\theta^2+mgl\cos\theta.
$$
Then
$$
\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\theta}=-mgl\sin\theta,\qquad
\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\dot\theta}=ml^2\dot\theta
\ \Longrightarrow\ \frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\dot\theta}
=ml^2\ddot\theta,
$$
and the Euler-Lagrange equation gives $ml^2\ddot\theta=-mgl\sin\theta$, i.e.
$$
\ddot\theta=-\frac{g}{l}\sin\theta,
$$
the familiar pendulum equation, obtained with no mention of the tension in the
rod. Here $ml^2\dot\theta$ is the angular momentum and $-mgl\sin\theta$ the
torque.

:::
